reading.title: How Writers Build a Mood
reading.purpose: See how the same place can feel joyful, lonely, or scary depending on the words a writer picks.
paras: Every story makes the reader feel something. That feeling is called the mood. Writers create it with the setting, the sounds, and the words they choose. The same place can feel completely different when the words change.

Picture a town square. A writer who wants a festive mood might describe bright banners, laughing families, and music. The atmosphere of the square would feel warm and full of joy. The word atmosphere also names the layer of gases around Earth, but here it means the feeling that fills a place.

Now change the square. Write about empty benches, a cold wind, and one flickering lamp, and the scene turns desolate, empty and lonely. If the sky grows dark gray and the wind rises, the mood becomes ominous, as if something bad is about to happen. Add a strange fog and a faint whistle, and the scene feels eerie.

Some moods are quieter. A somber mood is serious and sad, like a rainy day after a goodbye. A bleak scene is cold and dull, with no hope or comfort. A serene mood is calm and peaceful, like a lake at sunrise. A tense mood feels stretched tight, as when a character waits for important news.
To set a mood, choose details that match the feeling you want. Ask yourself which words would make a reader feel calm, or nervous, or ready to celebrate.

qs.q: In paragraph 3, the word "ominous" describes a scene that feels
choices: calm and peaceful, with no sign of any trouble
as if something bad is about to happen
empty and lonely, with no people or life nearby
full of joy, as if a celebration were about to begin
qs.why: The text explains it: an ominous mood is "as if something bad is about to happen."

qs.q: Which sentence shows the meaning of "atmosphere" that is used in this reading?
choices: A somber mood is serious and sad, like a rainy day after a goodbye.
A writer who wants a festive mood might describe bright banners, laughing families, and music.
The word atmosphere also names the layer of gases around Earth, but here it means the feeling that fills a place.
qs.why: This sentence separates the science meaning from the meaning used here: the feeling that fills a place.

ev.text: The word atmosphere also names the layer of gases around Earth, but here it means the feeling that fills a place.

qs.q: Why might a writer add "a strange fog and a faint whistle" to a scene?
choices: To make the reader feel that the place is crowded and cheerful
To show that the weather has finally become warm and sunny
To give the reader an uneasy, slightly scary feeling
To explain how a lamp can flicker in a cold wind
qs.why: The text says these details make the scene feel eerie, which is strange and a little scary.

qs.q: What is the main idea of this reading?
choices: Writers pick details and words that match the mood they want.
A town square is the only setting that can have a mood.
Every story should have a calm and peaceful atmosphere at the end.
Readers feel the same way no matter which words a writer uses.
qs.why: Each paragraph shows details that create a different mood, and the last one tells writers to choose details that match.

stretched tight, as when a character waits for important news
